# Part A · Getting Data from APIs

In Tutorials 1 and 2 we worked with datasets that R gave us ready-made (`mtcars`, the karate club). In real research, you usually have to **collect the data yourself**. Much of the data that interests digital sociologists lives on the web — social media, scholarly databases, open-source communities, government portals.

There are two doors to web data:

1.  **API** — an official door the site provides for programs. It returns structured data (usually **JSON**).
2.  **Web scraping** — when there is no API, you fetch the webpage itself (HTML, built for humans) and pull out the pieces you need.

> Rule of thumb: **use the API when there is one.** It is cleaner, more stable, and allowed by the site. Scraping is the fallback.

## 1. Install the tools

We need two packages today. Run the `install.packages()` lines only once (remove the `#` first time):

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# install.packages("httr2")   # talking to APIs
# install.packages("rvest")   # web scraping
# install.packages("jsonlite") # reading JSON (already used by httr2)
```

```{r}
library(httr2)
library(rvest)
library(jsonlite)
```

## 2. How the web works (30 seconds)

Every time you open a webpage, this happens:

- Your computer (**client**) sends an **HTTP request** to a **server**: "give me this page"
- The server sends back a **response**

A browser turns the response into a pretty page. But the response itself is just text in one of two languages:

- **HTML** — structure for humans: `<h3>`, `<p>`, `<table>`, …
- **JSON** — structure for programs: key–value pairs, like nested R lists

An **API** returns JSON. That is why it is so easy to work with in R.

## 3. JSON in one minute

JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) looks like this:

``` json
{
  "full_name": "igraph/rigraph",
  "stargazers_count": 195,
  "language": "R"
}
```

- `{ }` — an object (like an R **list**)
- `[ ]` — an array (like an R **vector**)
- Key–value pairs, can be nested inside each other

```{r}
# R's own version of the same data:
list(full_name = "igraph/rigraph", stargazers_count = 195, language = "R")
```

When we ask an API for data, `resp_body_json()` converts the JSON response into exactly this kind of R list. After that, it is just R: navigate with `$` and `[[ ]]`.

## 4. Calling an API from R

The modern package for HTTP requests is **`httr2`** (the older `httr` works similarly).

The three steps:

```{r}
# 1. build the request
req <- request("https://api.github.com/repos/igraph/rigraph")

# 2. perform it — send it to the server, get the response
resp <- req |> req_perform()
resp
```

```{r}
# 3. read the JSON body into an R list
repo <- resp |> resp_body_json()
repo$full_name
repo$stargazers_count
```

> `|>` (the pipe) passes the result on the left into the next function. `resp |> resp_body_json()` means `resp_body_json(resp)`.

Now that the data is an R list, you can do anything you like with it:

```{r}
# one-line summary of the whole repository record
str(repo, max.level = 1)
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 4. Calling an API from R - Note

The most important thing when you using APIs is **check the document from the provider**.

> Because they provide the interface.

- Cases - Tencent VOD: <https://www.tencentcloud.com/zh/document/product/266/34126> (with parameters)
- Openalex: <https://help.openalex.org/api/> (without parameters)

## 5. Example 1: GitHub API (no key needed)

GitHub hosts open-source projects — a social world of its own (who contributes to what, which projects are popular). Its API is free for basic queries.

Search for repositories matching a keyword:

```{r}
resp <- request("https://api.github.com/search/repositories") |>
  req_url_query(q = "sociology", sort = "stars", per_page = 10) |>
  req_perform()

repos <- resp |> resp_body_json()
```

Read the structure first:

```{r}
names(repos)            # total_count, items, ...
repos$total_count       # how many sociology repos exist on GitHub?
length(repos$items)     # how many did we get back? (per_page = 10)
```

Each element of `items` is one repository. Turn the list of lists into a data frame with `sapply()`:

```{r}
gh <- data.frame(
  repo     = sapply(repos$items, function(x) x$full_name),
  stars    = sapply(repos$items, function(x) x$stargazers_count),
  language = sapply(repos$items, function(x) x$language)
)
gh
```

```{r}
# which language is most common among the top repos?
table(gh$language)
```

## 6. Example 2: OpenAlex API (no key needed)

[OpenAlex](https://openalex.org/) is a free scholarly database covering papers, authors, institutions and citations. Very useful for social scientists — find literature, see who cites whom.

```{r}
resp <- request("https://api.openalex.org/works") |>
  req_url_query(search = "digital sociology", per_page = 10) |>
  req_perform()

works <- resp |> resp_body_json()

works$meta$count        # total matching works in the database
length(works$results)   # the first 10
```

Each work is a **nested** list — authors are inside `authorships`, which is a list of lists. Navigate step by step:

```{r}
w <- works$results[[1]]      # the first work
w$title
w$publication_year
w$cited_by_count

# authors: a list of authorship records; each has an "author" sub-list
length(w$authorships)
w$authorships[[1]]$author$display_name   # first author
```

Now build a data frame for all 10 works:

```{r}
title  <- sapply(works$results, function(w) w$title)
year   <- sapply(works$results, function(w) w$publication_year)
cites  <- sapply(works$results, function(w) w$cited_by_count)

# first author — must handle works with no authors
first_author <- sapply(works$results, function(w) {
  auth <- w$authorships
  if (length(auth) > 0) auth[[1]]$author$display_name else NA
})

papers <- data.frame(title = title, first_author = first_author,
                     year = year, citations = cites)
papers
```

```{r}
# which paper is the most cited?
papers[which.max(papers$citations), ]

# average publication year
mean(papers$year)
```

## 7. API keys & rate limits

- **Keys**: some APIs (Twitter/X, YouTube, NewsAPI) require you to register and get a key, which you add to each request. Never put a key in a script you share — a key is like a password.
- **Rate limits**: free APIs limit how many requests you can make. GitHub allows 60/hour without a key; the search endpoint only 10/minute. If you hit the limit you get an error (often 403).
- **Good manners**:
  - Identify yourself (User-Agent or `mailto=` parameter)
  - Don't re-download what you already have — save responses to a file
  - `Sys.sleep()` between requests in a loop

# Part B · Web Scraping

## 8. When there is no API

Most websites offer no API. But the data is there — inside the HTML that your browser renders. **Web scraping** means: fetch the page yourself and pull out the pieces you need.

> Analogy: the API is a served meal; scraping is cooking from the raw ingredients yourself.

For practice we use <http://books.toscrape.com/> — a fake bookstore **designed for practicing scraping**. Everything we do to it is welcome.

## 9. How a webpage is built

A page is HTML — tags give structure, classes and ids give names:

``` html
<article class="product_pod">
  <h3><a href="..." title="A Light in the Attic">A Light in the...</a></h3>
  <p class="price_color">£51.77</p>
  <p class="star-rating Three">...stars...</p>
</article>
```

To scrape, we need three things:

1.  Fetch the HTML: `read_html()`
2.  Select elements with a **CSS selector**: `html_elements()`
3.  Extract what we want: `html_text()`, `html_attr()`, `html_table()`

## 10. rvest basics

```{r}
# fetch and parse page 1 of the bookstore
html <- read_html("http://books.toscrape.com/")

html
```

Select all links inside `<h3>` headings and read their `title` attribute:

```{r}
html |> html_elements("h3 a") |> html_attr("title")
```

Prices: text inside elements with class `price_color`:

```{r}
html |> html_elements("p.price_color") |> html_text()
```

> **CSS selector cheat sheet**: `h3` (all `<h3>` tags) · `.price_color` (class) · `#main` (id) · `h3 a` (a inside h3) · `p.star-rating` (p with that class). Find selectors in your browser: right-click → Inspect, or use the SelectorGadget extension.

## 11. Example: page 1 of the bookstore

Goal: a data frame of all 20 books on page 1 with title, price and star rating.

```{r}
titles  <- html |> html_elements("h3 a") |> html_attr("title")
prices  <- html |> html_elements("p.price_color") |> html_text()
ratings <- html |> html_elements("p.star-rating") |> html_attr("class")
ratings <- gsub("star-rating ", "", ratings)   # "star-rating Three" -> "Three"

books <- data.frame(title = titles, price = prices, rating = ratings)
head(books)
```

Check that the three vectors have the same length — if one selector is wrong, lengths differ:

```{r}
length(titles); length(prices); length(ratings)
```

## 12. From text to numbers

Scraped data always arrives as **text**. Clean it before analyzing:

```{r}
books$price <- as.numeric(gsub("£", "", books$price))
books$price

mean(books$price)          # average price on page 1
table(books$rating)        # distribution of ratings
```

Once it is a clean data frame, all the Tutorial 1 & 2 tools apply — plots, models, networks.

## 13. Pagination: scraping several pages

The bookstore has 50 pages. Page 1 is the homepage; pages 2–50 live at `catalogue/page-N.html`. Because the URL is just a string, we can loop over it:

```{r}
books_all <- data.frame()

for (i in 1:3) {
  url <- if (i == 1) "http://books.toscrape.com/" else
         paste0("http://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/page-", i, ".html")

  page <- read_html(url)
  Sys.sleep(1)   # be polite: wait 1 second between requests

  titles  <- page |> html_elements("h3 a") |> html_attr("title")
  prices  <- page |> html_elements("p.price_color") |> html_text()
  ratings <- page |> html_elements("p.star-rating") |> html_attr("class")
  ratings <- gsub("star-rating ", "", ratings)

  page_df <- data.frame(title = titles, price = prices, rating = ratings)
  books_all <- rbind(books_all, page_df)
}

books_all$price <- as.numeric(gsub("£", "", books_all$price))
nrow(books_all)
```

## 14. Ethics & legality

Scraping is a request like any other — what makes it right or wrong is **how** you do it:

- Check **robots.txt** first — <http://books.toscrape.com/robots.txt> explicitly welcomes crawlers; many real sites restrict parts of themselves
- Respect the site's **Terms of Service** — some forbid scraping entirely
- **Don't hammer** the server: `Sys.sleep()`, cache what you download, don't re-request
- Scraped data ≠ free data: **copyright** and **personal data** protections still apply
- Same research ethics as any data collection: privacy, consent, purpose
- When in doubt: ask the site owner, or use an official API/dataset

**Dynamic pages (advanced)**: some sites build their content with JavaScript after the page loads, so `read_html()` sees an empty shell. Options: (1) find the API the page itself calls — DevTools → Network tab; (2) drive a real browser with `chromote` or `playwright`; (3) `RSelenium`. For this course, prefer sites that render in plain HTML.

## Hands-on

**Task A · APIs:**

1.  GitHub — search repositories for "sociology", sorted by stars. Which repository has the most stars? Which language is most common among the top 10?
2.  OpenAlex — fetch 10 works matching "digital sociology". Build a data frame of title, year and citations. Which paper is the most cited? What is the average publication year?
3.  Challenge — OpenAlex gives nested author lists. Extract the **first author** of each work too.

**Task B · Web scraping:**

1.  Scrape books.toscrape.com page 1: title, price, rating → data frame
2.  Extend to pages 1–3 with a loop (remember `Sys.sleep()`!)
3.  With the combined data frame: average price? most common rating? any pattern between price and rating (e.g. `boxplot(price ~ rating)`)?

**Do:** the hands-on exercises end-to-end on your own machine.

> **Network slow or blocked?** The materials folder contains cached copies so you can keep working offline: `books_page1.html`, `openalex_digital_sociology.json`, `github_sociology_repos.json`. Load them with `read_html("books_page1.html")` and `fromJSON("openalex_digital_sociology.json")` — everything else is the same.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# offline fallback demo
html_offline <- read_html("books_page1.html")      # same selectors work
works_offline <- fromJSON("openalex_digital_sociology.json")  # same $ navigation
```

**Task C · Scraping data by using LLMs:**

1.  set prompting

"I would like to scrape the **research interests** of all the professors listed on this webpage: <https://www.soc.cuhk.edu.hk/people/faculty/>. Could you provide me with some R code to do this?"

```{r}
# Install packages if needed:
# install.packages(c("rvest", "stringr", "dplyr", "purrr", "readr", "tibble"))

library(rvest)
library(stringr)
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(readr)
library(tibble)

url <- "https://www.soc.cuhk.edu.hk/people/faculty/"

# 1. Download the webpage and extract text while preserving line breaks
page <- read_html(url)

lines <- page |>
  html_element("body") |>
  html_text2() |>
  str_split("\\n") |>
  unlist() |>
  str_squish()

# Remove empty lines
lines <- lines[nzchar(lines)]

# 2. Exclude the Lecturers section and everything after it
lecturers_position <- which(
  str_detect(lines, regex("^Lecturers$", ignore_case = TRUE))
)

if (length(lecturers_position) > 0L) {
  lines <- lines[seq_len(lecturers_position[1] - 1L)]
}

# 3. Locate professor titles, including assistant and associate professors
title_pattern <- paste0(
  "^(?:(?:Chair\\s+and|Vice-Chancellor|Assistant|Associate)\\s+)?",
  "Professor$"
)

title_positions <- which(
  str_detect(lines, regex(title_pattern, ignore_case = TRUE))
)

if (length(title_positions) == 0L) {
  stop(
    "No professor titles found. Check whether the page loaded correctly ",
    "or whether its structure has changed."
  )
}

# 4. Locate each faculty member's English name
# Expected order: English name, optional Chinese name, title, research interests
name_positions <- map_int(title_positions, function(position) {
  previous <- position - 1L

  if (previous < 1L) {
    stop("Unexpected page structure: no name found before a professor title.")
  }

  # If the preceding line contains only a Chinese name,
  # the English name should be one line earlier
  chinese_name_only <- str_detect(lines[previous], "\\p{Han}") &&
    !str_detect(lines[previous], "[A-Za-z]")

  name_position <- if (chinese_name_only) previous - 1L else previous

  if (name_position < 1L) {
    stop("Unexpected page structure: English name could not be located.")
  }

  name_position
})

# 5. Extract each faculty member's details from their text block
faculty <- map_dfr(seq_along(title_positions), function(i) {
  title_position <- title_positions[i]
  name_position <- name_positions[i]

  # Each block ends immediately before the next faculty member's name
  block_end <- if (i < length(title_positions)) {
    name_positions[i + 1L] - 1L
  } else {
    length(lines)
  }

  block <- lines[seq.int(title_position, block_end)]

  interests_position <- which(
    str_detect(
      block,
      regex("^Research Interests\\s*:?", ignore_case = TRUE)
    )
  )

  research_interests <- NA_character_

  if (length(interests_position) > 0L) {
    label_position <- interests_position[1]

    # Handle interests appearing on the same line as the label
    same_line <- str_remove(
      block[label_position],
      regex("^Research Interests\\s*:?\\s*", ignore_case = TRUE)
    )

    # Collect any additional lines following the label
    following_lines <- if (label_position < length(block)) {
      block[seq.int(label_position + 1L, length(block))]
    } else {
      character()
    }

    research_interests <- str_squish(
      paste(c(same_line, following_lines), collapse = " ")
    )

    if (!nzchar(research_interests)) {
      research_interests <- NA_character_
    }
  }

  # Extract the optional Chinese name
  chinese_name <- if (name_position + 1L < title_position) {
    paste(
      lines[seq.int(name_position + 1L, title_position - 1L)],
      collapse = " "
    )
  } else {
    NA_character_
  }

  tibble(
    name = lines[name_position],
    chinese_name = chinese_name,
    title = lines[title_position],
    research_interests = research_interests
  )
})

# Optional: keep only full professors
# faculty <- faculty |>
#   filter(title %in% c("Professor", "Chair and Professor"))

# 6. Display the results
print(faculty, n = Inf, width = Inf)

# 7. Save a CSV with a UTF-8 BOM for compatibility with Excel
output_file <- "cuhk_sociology_professors.csv"
write_excel_csv(faculty, output_file)

cat("\nExtracted", nrow(faculty), "faculty members.\n")
cat("Saved to:", file.path(getwd(), output_file), "\n")

# Warn if any research interests are missing
if (anyNA(faculty$research_interests)) {
  warning(
    "Research interests are missing for some faculty members. ",
    "Check the webpage structure."
  )
}
```
